# Same Word of HTML Labels

## Problem

You are given the roots of two N‑ary trees, where each tree models a hierarchical label layout similar to HTML elements. Each label can have one of two configurations:

- It holds a **non‑empty string value** and has zero children (a leaf).
- It holds **no string value** (its `text` is empty or null) and acts purely as a container that groups one or more child labels in top‑to‑bottom order.

A **leaf label** is defined as any label that contains a non‑empty string and does not possess any children. Every other label is a structural grouping element; its `text` should be treated as empty.

Your job is to walk each tree and collect the text values of all leaf labels from top to bottom. Concatenate them in the order they are encountered within the layout.

Return `true` if the final concatenated strings from the two label structures are **identical** (same case and character sequence). Return `false` otherwise.

The label node is represented by the following class:

```java
class HtmlLabel {
    String text;
    List<HtmlLabel> children;
    ...
}
```

**Constraints**

- Every leaf label carries a non‑empty string of at most 100 characters.
- The top‑to‑bottom ordering of children must be preserved when traversing.
- 0 ≤ total number of labels in either structure ≤ 10^5.

**Example**

> **Input:**
>
```
> Label 1:
> <root>
>   <container>
>     <div> "He" </div>
>     <div> "llo" </div>
>   </container>
>   <p> "World" </p>
> </root>
>
> Label 2:
> <root>
>   <div> "Hello" </div>
>   <container>
>     <span> "Wor" </span>
>     <span> "ld" </span>
>   </container>
> </root>
>
```
>
> **Output:**
> true
>
> **Explanation:**
> - First structure leaf labels in order: "He" + "llo" + "World" → "HelloWorld".
> - Second structure leaf labels in order: "Hello" + "Wor" + "ld" → "HelloWorld".
>
> The concatenated strings are equal, so the result is true.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Think of the problem as checking whether two trees represent the same sequence of leaf strings when you flatten them using a left-to-right depth-first traversal.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a recursive traversal that collects leaf text values from both trees and compare the resulting lists, ignoring internal container nodes that have no text.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

Your solution should run in O(N) time where N is the total number of nodes across both trees.

</details>
